thread.title: Salesforce Duo Makes the Case for Co-CEOs in Tech

author: Jon Swartz
title: Salesforce Duo Makes the Case for Co-CEOs in Tech
text:
Keith Block and Marc Benioff Photo: Courtesy of Salesforce By Jon Swartz Aug. 31, 2018 5:16 p.m. ET The age-old axiom that two heads are better than one has rarely worked in the office of the chief executive at tech companies.
One by one, co-CEO experiments have fizzled, if not outright flopped. Research In Motion, now BlackBerry (ticker: BB) crashed and burned by 2012 when Jim Balsillie and Mike Lazaridis, who had equally divided corporate and product strategy, faced the dual onslaught of Apple’s iPhone and Google’s Android. SAP (SAP) gave the so-called “two-in-a-box” strategy a go from 2010-14 with moderate success, before it settled on Bill McDermott, who remains its sole CEO. Oracle (ORCL) has lagged behind its competition in the fast-moving cloud and software industries since 2014 behind the two-headed CEO of Safra Catz and Mark Hurd. (Company co-founder Larry Ellison, who abdicated his role as CEO but remains hands on, is chief technology officer.)
Indeed, Fortune calculates that only 23 companies in the Fortune 500 over the past three decades have tackled a co-CEO model. If baseball doubleheaders are rare, tech companies run by two CEOs seem to be virtually nonexistent.
So when Salesforce.com (CRM) said it had elevated Keith Block, its long-time chief operating officer, to share CEO duties with company co-founder Marc Benioff, how did the market react? It sent Salesforce shares up 5% after the promotion was announced on Aug. 8.
The Benioff-Block stewardship, which has been in effect since 2013, received another boost from investors on Wednesday, when Salesforce reported $3.28 billion in fiscal 2019 second-quarter revenue, a 27% jump from the same quarter a year ago. “Benioff has built a multicloud company from a single product, and Block built the operational, go-to sales model that helped the company blossom,” says Joel Fishbein, BTIG managing director, software and cloud technology .
Fishbein, who wrote two positive notes on Salesforce this week, has reiterated a Buy rating on its stock, and raised his target price to $175 from $140. “They have created a truly dynamic partnership,” he says.
By nearly every measure, the tandem has worked. As Benioff himself says, “Cementing our leadership strengthens Salesforce’s ability to continue our extraordinary in a way consistent with our values.”
The charismatic billionaire Benioff, who can be as bold as his Hawaiian shirts, and the buttoned-down Block, the steadying COO since 2016, have co-piloted the company’s annual revenue beyond $10 billion in its 2018 fiscal year—a feat it accomplished faster than any other enterprise-software company—and are on pace to eclipse $13 billion in fiscal 2019. The next goal: $23 billion in sales by fiscal 2022.
More on Salesforce Salesforce Revenue Proves That 2 Heads Are Better Than 1 Salesforce Names COO Keith Block co-CEO Salesforce Can Reach New Heights on Cloud Since the duo teamed up in 2013, Salesforce’s annualized five-year revenue growth is four times that of rivals SAP, at 7.7%, and Microsoft (MSFT), at 7.2%. Oracle has grown revenue at an annualized 1.4% over the past five years. The disparity is just as pronounced over the past 12 months, through Thursday’s close. Salesforce shares are up 60%, exceeding those of Microsoft (51%), SAP (13%), and Oracle (-4%).
“This is an extension of what we’ve already been doing—leveraging each other’s strengths and advising each other,” says Block, 57 . In his new role, Block, who remains a board member, reports to the full board, not to Benioff. Their duties have been clear cut for a few years. Playing to their strengths, Benioff oversees technology, products, and culture; Block handles growth strategy, execution, and operations. “Weirdly, tech is the one place you can justify it,” Box (BOX) CEO Aaron Levie says . “Essentially, you need a balance in personality and characteristics for two such different tasks as head of product strategy versus operations.”
Some analysts compare the Salesforce arrangement to Apple’s succession plan from CEO Steve Jobs, who died in October 2011, to operations whiz Tim Cook, who remains in charge. “Block is being groomed by Benioff as his Cook, a CEO-in-training who happens to excel at operations,” Daniel Newman, principal analyst at Futurum Research + Analysis, says . “Benioff, at 53, has been doing this a long time. He’s more interested in strategy. He’s on the path to being a chairman, a more passive role.”
Benioff has said he has no intention of retiring soon.
The American myth of the heroic CEO often obscures the collaborative nature of most tech companies, notes Paul Maeder, founding partner at Highland Capital Partners . “Most great companies were built by two people with complementary skills: Microsoft, Google, Hewlett-Packard, Intel (INTC), eBay (EBAY),” he says. Though they’re invariably driven by visionary founders, it takes an organizational expert to scale the business. “You better have complementary roles, or people will wonder who’s in charge,” says GoDaddy (GIDDY) CEO Scott Wagner, who as COO teamed up with former CEO Blake Irving to build the domain-name company into a $2.5 billion business.
Newsletter Sign-up Taking the concept further, once those companies are established, they are often run by two people—“one, an artist, the other a good business head,” says University of Alabama professor Patrick J. Murphy. “You need to translate crazy ideas into a sound business plan.” Murphy points to successful “two-headed” partnerships at Apple (AAPL) and Facebook (FB). The sticking point, he says, comes when a non-CEO aspires to be the leader, creating ego clashes and fights over direction.
And there could be another reason for Block’s promotion at Salesforce: It reduces the chance of him bolting for another CEO job, Newman and others say. In fact, being the boss and creating a company is what drove then 34-year-old Benioff to leave Oracle after 13 years to start Salesforce in a rented San Francisco apartment in 1999. Block himself decamped from Oracle in 2013 after a dispute with Hurd and joined Salesforce as vice chairman after a long and impressive career.
